transcript: Hello, this is John Sarbanes. Thank you for tuning in to Commuting to Congress. The online reflections of a lawmaker who by day gets an insider's view of the nation's capital and at night leaves the DC bubble and heads back home to the district. Today I wanted to talk about the McCutcheon case which is a case of Supreme Court in the last few days decided to take It's a case that challenges the current limits that are put in place for the amount that a single contributor can give to all federal campaigns. These are limits that have been in place for decades. And the fact that the court has taken this case causes me great concern because we've seen what they did with the Citizens United case recently in terms of beginning to take limits off of what happens in the funding of our campaigns. The challenge in this case is to rules that say that the total amount of money that can be given across all congressional campaigns and federal campaigns by a single donor is $123,000. And if the Supreme Court decides to lift that limit, they might also go further and lift the limit on the amount that can be contributed to a single candidate from a contributor, which is now $2,600 in a primary and $2,600 in a general election. If they do that, if they take those limits off, then Sheldon Adelson's of the world can come in and give $200,000 to one candidate. And that will only contribute further to the perception that the public has that lawmakers basically are being owned by the special interests and aren't responding to the concerns of the average person out there. It's why I'm pushing so hard to try to reform the way we fund campaigns and at least create an option for candidates, grassroots candidates to go out there, build support from grassroots donors and have that support matched with public dollars to amplify their voice. I've introduced the Grassroots Democracy Act, which we do just that. We're going to keep up the fight. to try to promote grassroots, funded, citizen-owned campaigns. And at the end of the day, it comes down to the fundamental question, who's going to own your government? Is it going to be special interest and big money? In which case, when it comes time to make policy, that's the direction the institutions of Congress will lean towards. Or is it going to be the average person? Is it going to be you, the folks who can make a contribution of five, ten, fifteen dollars? And in return, just ask that their government respond to their interests and not the special interests. We'll keep up that fight. I appreciate your being connected to this issue as we move forward, this issue of money and politics. Again, I'd like to thank you for tuning into Commuting to Congress. If you have any questions about this episode or have an idea for an episode you'd like me to do in the future, Please email me at info at johnsorbanes.com. Send me a tweet at johnsorbanes or post your idea on my Facebook page. Thank you.

explicit_propositions.text: John Sarbanes is speaking on 'Commuting to Congress'.
The McCutcheon case involves the Supreme Court reviewing limits on campaign contributions.
Current law limits a single donor to $123,000 across all federal campaigns.
There is a separate limit of $2,600 per candidate per election cycle.
John Sarbanes supports reforming campaign finance through the Grassroots Democracy Act.
Lifting contribution limits may increase perceptions that lawmakers serve special interests over ordinary citizens.
The Grassroots Democracy Act matches small donations with public funds to amplify grassroots voices.
If the Supreme Court lifts the aggregate limit, it could lead to lifting individual candidate limits.
Campaign finance reform aims to ensure government responds to average citizens rather than special interests.
Sheldon Adelson could potentially donate $200,000 to a single candidate if limits were removed.

assumptions.text: Public trust in democratic institutions depends on perceived independence from wealthy donors.
A government responsive to small donors reflects democratic values better than one shaped by large contributors.
Large contributions inherently undermine equal political representation.
Big-money influence leads to predictable policy outcomes favorable to elite interests.
Average citizens are more representative of national interests than wealthy individuals or corporations.
The Supreme Court’s decision-making is influenced by ideological bias favoring deregulation of campaign finance.
Donors like Sheldon Adelson represent a class whose influence distorts democratic processes.
Grassroots fundraising with public matching increases legitimacy and responsiveness of elected officials.
The public expects politicians to prioritize constituents' needs over donor preferences.
Campaign finance laws are effective tools for maintaining fair electoral competition.
